name: Affirmations / self-talk

image.caption: 130424 Image of Positive Mindset Affirmations on Making a Difference

lead: Affirmations are positive statements people repeat or write to change how they see themselves, often used to counter negative face or body image. The payoff is a softer self-image and a more relaxed, confident presence.

Self-affirmation theory, proposed by Claude Steele in 1988, holds that reflecting on valued domains protects overall self-worth and reduces defensiveness under threat; it has produced experimental findings on stress. Repeating positive statements is a separate practice: a 2009 study by Wood and colleagues found present-tense statements such as 'I am...' helped people with high self-esteem but left those with low self-esteem feeling worse. No studies have tested affirmations for appearance outcomes.

paras: People repeat or write statements daily, often in the morning or in front of a mirror, in present tense and personalised to them. Some choose value-based reflection, writing about what matters to them, instead of statements about looks.
No physical risks are documented. Studies suggest present-tense positive statements may worsen mood for people with low self-esteem.

social.title: Positive Affirmations for Women and Men

angle.text: Users repeat positive statements to counter negative face or body image, aiming for a softer self-image and a more relaxed, confident presence. Value-based self-affirmation has research on stress and defensiveness; affirmations for looks have not been tested.

lead: Affirmations and positive self-talk are mental practices in which a person repeats or writes encouraging statements, or reflects on core values, to shift how they see themselves. In looks-related use, people apply them to counter harsh judgments of their face and body, aiming for steadier confidence that shows up as better posture, eye contact and presence.[1][2][3]

Two bodies of work are often combined. Self-affirmation theory, proposed by Claude Steele in 1988, concerns reflecting on important values to protect self-worth, and has produced experiments on stress and defensiveness.[2][4] Repeating positive statements is a separate practice from the New Thought tradition. A 2009 study by Wood and colleagues reported that 'I am' statements helped people with high self-esteem but left those with low self-esteem feeling worse.[1]

Sport psychology has its own literature on self-talk: a meta-analysis of 32 studies reported a moderate positive effect on task performance,[5] and a randomized trial found motivational self-talk lengthened time to exhaustion in endurance cycling.[6] Self-affirmation has also been tested for appearance-related health behaviour such as sun protection.[7] No study has tested affirmations for facial or physical appearance outcomes.

paras: Practitioners use written or spoken statements, sometimes with images, mantra chanting or hypnosis.[1] The practice is associated with Wallace Wattles' 1910 The Science of Getting Rich, Napoleon Hill, Rhonda Byrne's The Secret (2006) and Louise Hay's 1984 You Can Heal Your Life.[1] Some teachers suggest using affirmations when already feeling calm, or pairing them with acknowledgements of steps already taken.[1]

Self-affirmation theory holds that people defend their overall sense of adequacy, and that reflecting on a valued domain makes threats easier to handle.[2] Studies reported lower cortisol responses to a lab stressor (Creswell 2005), reduced stress-related performance drops (Creswell 2013) and greater acceptance of health-risk messages (Sherman 2000).[2] Education studies by Cohen and colleagues (2006, 2009) reported narrower achievement gaps, and Logel and Cohen (2012) reported greater weight loss among affirmed women.[2] Limitations include unclear mechanisms, mixed effects on mood and self-esteem, cultural differences, and benefits mainly when the threatened area mattered to the person; Cohen and Sherman (2014) call the stress findings preliminary.[2]

The 2009 Wood study found that people with low self-esteem fared better with statements that allowed for doubt or were future-tense ('I will').[1] A 2016 fMRI study linked self-affirmation to reward-related brain regions, and recent work suggests affirmations combined with mindfulness may aid emotional regulation.[1]

A meta-analysis of 32 studies (62 effect sizes) found a positive moderate effect of self-talk on sport task performance.[5] A systematic review of 47 studies reported beneficial effects of positive, instructional and motivational self-talk.[8] In a randomized trial, motivational self-talk reduced perceived effort and extended time to exhaustion in endurance cycling.[6] A 2014 set of seven studies found that referring to oneself by name or with non-first-person pronouns during introspection improved responses under social stress.[9]
Lifters describing their own training sometimes mention self-talk as part of getting through hard sessions, which connects the practice to building a stronger physique.[10]

Wikipedia's article on body image links poor body image with lower self-esteem and with attempts to change the body through dieting or cosmetic surgery, and describes interventions such as school body-confidence lessons and body-positive media.[3] Self-affirmation interventions have been tested on appearance-linked behaviour: randomized trials have examined affirmation approaches for sun protection and for reducing defensiveness toward health-risk messages.[7][11] Belief in manifestation, a related idea, has been examined in a 2025 psychology paper.[12]

No studies found testing affirmations for physical appearance outcomes. Related randomized trials and reviews cover self-affirmation for stress, performance and health behaviour,[4][7][11] and self-talk for sport performance.[5][6][8]

lore.intro: Affirmations appear in training and self-improvement forums as a mindset tool, usually described in terms of motivation and confidence.[10]

claims.claim: Positive self-talk helps you push harder and stay confident
